problem_markdown: Fix a point $P$ inside a sphere of radius $R$ and centre $O$. Three mutually perpendicular rays from $P$ meet the sphere at $U,V,W$. Complete the rectangular box with edges $PU,PV,PW$, and let $Q$ be opposite $P$. Determine the full locus of $Q$.
solutions_markdown:
The locus is the sphere centred at $O$ with radius $\sqrt{3R^2-2OP^2}$.

Take $O$ as origin, write $p=\overrightarrow{OP}$, and put $c=R^2-|p|^2>0$. Let the three unit directions be $e_i$ and edge lengths $t_i$. The sphere equations give $t_i^2+2t_i(p\cdot e_i)=c$. For $q=p+\sum t_ie_i$, adding gives $|q|^2=|p|^2+3c$.

Conversely take any $q$ with that norm. Define $H(e)=(q\cdot e)^2-(p\cdot e)^2$ on unit vectors. Its values on every orthonormal triple sum to $3c$. Start with any such triple; its minimum and maximum values bracket $c$, so continuity along a spherical path supplies a unit $e_1$ with $H(e_1)=c$. On the perpendicular plane, the values at perpendicular unit vectors sum to $2c$; continuity around its unit circle supplies $e_2$ with value $c$, and its perpendicular $e_3$ then also has value $c$.

Orient each $e_i$ so that $t_i=(q-p)\cdot e_i>0$. This is possible because $H(e_i)=c>0$ rules out $t_i=0$. The equation $H(e_i)=c$ becomes $t_i^2+2t_i(p\cdot e_i)=c$, so $p+t_ie_i$ lies on the original sphere. These rays yield exactly $q$, proving the converse.
